composition: Nominal composition 12Al-10Mn-1C (wt%) within the studied Fe–Mn–Al–C family, whose overall ranges are Al 9–12 wt%, Mn 10–20–30 wt%, C 0.4–1 wt%, Fe balance (Table 1). Aluminium is the main density-reducing element (alloying at least 16 wt% Al enables more than 20% density reduction; Al is also a strong κ-carbide former and raises the Al–C chemical driving force for κ-carbide precipitation). Manganese and carbon are added as austenite stabilizers to improve microstructure and mechanical properties; Al also enhances microstructural ordering, which is why Mn/C additions are needed. In this grade the 10 wt% Mn and 1 wt% C are not sufficient to stabilize austenite against its own decomposition, and the high 12 wt% Al provides an enhanced driving force that makes the reaction affect the entire γ volume.
conclusions: For 12Al-10Mn-1C tempered at 600 °C, austenite decomposition is classified as a "generic precipitation transformation" — a random-like reaction, not as ordered and defined as discontinuous precipitation — that involved the whole γ volume and was linked only to slight hardening effects (hot-rolled 401 HV → 600 °C tempered 420 HV, an increase of 19 HV). Unlike the 9Al-10Mn-1C alloy, whose 600 °C treatment produces γ + κ fine lamellae by discontinuous precipitation with narrow inter-lamellar spacing and strong hardening (273 → 439 HV), the 12Al-10Mn-1C grade develops no γ + κ-carbide lamellar structures but an austenite matrix with carbon-depleted γ regions and globular κ-carbides, plus strong κ-carbide precipitation along δ/γ boundaries and poor precipitation within ferrite; the absence of random lamellar phases was considered to ensure a more solid microstructure configuration. Broadly, the paper shows that 600 °C tempering triggers slight/incipient transformations (discontinuous precipitation and precipitation transformation) while 800 °C triggers complete and widespread transformations (cellular transformation coupled with spinodal decomposition), and that the limiting conditions for each reaction are set by the combination of chemical driving force (Al, C), thermal energy input and the thermodynamic stability of austenite (Mn, C). Fitting into this framework, the 12% Al content gives an enhanced driving force relative to the 9Al alloys, which is the reason the reaction spreads through the whole γ volume at 600 °C.
mechanisms: Thermal energy input at 600 °C tempering accelerates the reaction kinetics and establishes altered thermodynamic conditions for γ stability relative to the hot-rolled state, providing the driving force and reaction velocity needed to trigger austenite decomposition.

Raising Al to 12 wt% increases the Al–C chemical driving force for κ-carbide formation and shifts the phase equilibria (the f.c.c. field moves toward higher temperatures and away from the tempering temperature), so that the 600 °C reaction involves the whole γ volume rather than producing partial discontinuous precipitation as in the 9Al counterpart.

Because 10 wt% Mn and 1 wt% C are not high enough to stabilize austenite against its own transformation at 600 °C, γ decomposes into a carbon-depleted γ0 variant plus κ-carbide through a complex, random-like 'generic precipitation transformation' instead of an ordered discontinuous precipitation that would consume the parent phase from grain boundaries.

Carbon depletion during the transformation creates two austenite grades that appear as alternated bands; globular κ-carbides nucleate and grow only inside the carbon-depleted γ variant, not in the other austenite grade, which is direct evidence that carbon depletion controls where κ forms.

κ-carbide precipitation is strong along δ/γ boundaries but poor inside ferrite, so the δ/γ interfaces act as preferential nucleation sites for the carbide while the ferritic constituent is largely inert to κ precipitation.

The absence of 'random' lamellar γ + κ phases gives a more solid microstructural configuration, and the transformation proceeds without the lamellar morphology that would otherwise produce strong hardening; this is why this state shows only slight hardening (401 → 420 HV, +19 HV) compared with the narrow-spacing discontinuous-precipitation lamellae of 9Al-10Mn-1C tempered at 600 °C (273 → 439 HV).

Tempering at 600 °C supplies lower thermal energy than 800 °C, so the reactions here remain slight/incipient, whereas 800 °C accelerates kinetics enough to drive complete and widespread cellular transformation coupled with spinodal decomposition.
microstructure: Tempering at 600 °C caused the whole γ volume to pass through a complex, random-like transformation ("generic precipitation transformation") that is less ordered and defined than discontinuous precipitation. No classical γ + κ-carbide lamellar (discontinuous-precipitation) structure was detected; instead the microstructure consists of an austenite matrix (γ, f.c.c./FCC_A1) characterized by carbon-depleted γ regions carrying globular κ-carbide nodules, together with alternated bands of what appear to be two different austenite grades (one of them the carbon-depleted γ0 variant), plus δ-ferrite (b.c.c. δ). Globular κ-carbides precipitated within the carbon-depleted γ regions but not in the other austenite grade. Precipitation of κ-carbide was strong along δ/γ boundaries, whereas κ-carbide precipitation within ferrite was poor. Micrographs of this state (Fig. 3(b), SE-SEM at 20 kV, ×10,000, 1 µm scale bar; Fig. 4, BSE-SEM, 100 µm scale bar) show a strongly banded, lath-like structure in which light elongated parallel bands (labelled γ+κ lamellae) alternate with darker matrix regions (labelled γα + coarse κ). The paper states that the absence of "random" lamellar phases ensured a more solid microstructure configuration. No grain size, texture or volume-fraction values are reported for this state.
processing: Processing sequence: (1) casting in a 100 kW vacuum induction furnace under vacuum, producing 0.5 kg ingots; (2) hot-rolling of the ingots at 1150 °C to 5 mm thick flat products; (3) water quenching after hot-rolling; (4) tempering (heat treatment) at 600 °C for 30 min; (5) water quenching after tempering. This 600 °C/30 min + water-quench tempering is the step that defines the present sample; the hot-rolled + water-quenched state is its precursor and benchmark condition. Specimens for microscopy were through-thickness embedded, ground and polished separately for the hot-rolled and heat-treated conditions.
properties: Vickers macro-hardness of the 600 °C tempered bulk: 420 HV (5 kg load for all indentations, 5 indentations per sample, through-thickness embedded and polished specimens). The hot-rolled benchmark of the same alloy is 401 HV, so the 600 °C tempering produced only a slight hardening of +19 HV. No tensile, fracture-toughness, fatigue, creep, physical, chemical or radiation properties are reported for this sample. Characterization techniques applied to the alloy at this condition: optical microscopy (all processing conditions), scanning electron microscopy in secondary-electron (SEI) and back-scattered-electron modes on selected microstructures (e.g. Fig. 3(b) at 20 kV, ×10,000, 1 µm scale bar; Fig. 4 BSE-SEM, 100 µm scale bar), SEM-EDS/EDX for qualitative local phase composition, Vickers macro-hardness testing, and supporting CALPHAD phase-volume-fraction diagrams. Minitab18® software was used to check data consistency and exclude outliers.
summary: 12Al-10Mn-1C is a medium-Mn, high-Al, high-C Fe–Mn–Al–C lightweight steel (nominal 12 wt% Al, 10 wt% Mn, 1 wt% C, Fe balance) that was vacuum-induction cast, hot-rolled at 1150 °C to 5 mm flat product, water quenched, then tempered at 600 °C for 30 min and water quenched. The research question addressed is how austenite decomposes in this quaternary system as a function of composition and heat-treatment temperature; at 600 °C this alloy undergoes a "generic precipitation transformation" of the whole γ volume (γ → carbon-depleted γ + globular κ-carbide) instead of an ordered discontinuous precipitation, giving only slight hardening (401 → 420 HV).
unmapped: The banded lath-like morphology published for this sample (Fig. 4 BSE-SEM, 100 µm scale bar) is annotated with 'γ+κ lamellae' and 'γα + coarse κ' bands, which is difficult to reconcile with the text statement that γ + κ-carbide lamellar structures were not detected in 12Al-10Mn-1C tempered at 600 °C; the banded features should therefore be read together with the text conclusion that the state consists of an austenite matrix with carbon-depleted regions and globular κ-carbides.

The EDS table presented alongside this figure (Table 3) is titled for 9Al-10Mn-1C tempered at 600 °C whereas the figure caption names 12Al-10Mn-1C, so the numerical EDS data (Al and Mn in δ, γ, κ and γ nano-κ) cannot be unambiguously attributed to this sample.

The SEM micrograph grouped in Fig. 3 ('heat treatment at 600 °C') is captioned jointly for 2Al-10Mn-0.4C and 12Al-10Mn-1C; only one panel is available and its assignment to one or the other composition cannot be established from the image alone.

The paper's fourth transformation type, spinodal decomposition (γ → γ0 + γ′ → γ0 + L12 → γ0 + L12/E21), and the cellular transformation products (α + κ or α + κ + γ0 lamellae) are discussed for 800 °C tempered alloys only and are not observed in this 600 °C tempered sample.
